extracted.intended_audience: law professors, practicing lawyers, and journalists interested in editorial ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and cautionary standards for editors and lawyers about verifying sources, preserving evidence, and maintaining professional skepticism, drawn from the Janet Cooke/‘Jimmy’s World’ scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must insist on knowing and verifying
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have to insist on knowing and verifying (names, addresses, identifying information) rather than relying on blanket promises of confidentiality or absolute trust in reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bill Green: 'Editors have to insist on knowing and verifying.' Do not accept reporters' assurances in lieu of basic identifying facts; insist on documentation and verifiable details even when sources are promised confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let promises of anonymity prevent verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering anonymity or confidentiality to sources should not preclude editors from pressing for identifying information or independent confirmation of key facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post's error began when an editor allowed Cooke to grant anonymity and then stopped asking for the mother's name or family street address. Editors should require alternative verification if a source must remain anonymous (e.g., corroboration, independent witnesses, records).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and inspect reporters' original notes and recordings
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain reporters' raw materials (notes, tapes) and inspect them when questions arise; the absence of corroborating material can be decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooke's notes and tape recordings, when reviewed, contained no mention of 'Jimmy' — the absence of evidence exposed the fraud. Newsrooms should retain originals so editors can verify claims and detect fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify reporters' credentials and background claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm factual claims on a reporter's resume or biography, because discrepancies can undermine credibility and cast doubt on reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Toledo Blade discovered Cooke had lied about degrees and honors; that discovery prompted scrutiny of her reporting. Editors should independently check credentials, especially before elevating a reporter's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to implausibilities and ask for corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: When experts, officials, or knowledgeable observers raise doubts about a story's plausibility, editors should demand confirmation, documentation, or prior consistent statements instead of defending the piece by default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts and the mayor expressed skepticism about the likelihood of a child addict allowing a reporter to observe; instead of insisting on confirmation, editors stood by the story. Press for concrete evidence when reasonable people call a claim into question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being seduced by a 'too good to be true' narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that are especially well-written or compelling can suppress editors' skepticism; recognize narrative appeal as a cognitive bias that requires extra verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bob Woodward: 'This story was so well-written and tied together so well... my alarm bells simply didn’t go off.' Treat unusually tidy narratives with heightened scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-editor vetting must be active, not passive
rubrics_metrics.description: Having an extensive vetting process with many editors is insufficient unless those editors actively verify facts and press reporters; passive review can still fail to catch fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post had multiple reviewers (including high-profile editors) yet the process failed because editors relied on trust rather than verification. Vetting protocols should include concrete verification steps and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to public inquiries and doubts with renewed investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: When readers and the public raise questions, editors should re-examine the underlying evidence instead of invoking First Amendment or source-protection defenses to avoid scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After telephones began ringing and doubts surfaced publicly, editors did not insist on confirmation. Public scrutiny should trigger renewed verification efforts, not defensive posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional skepticism as a cross-field duty (lawyers included)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals (e.g., lawyers) should cultivate ingrained skepticism — testing facts through adversarial methods (cross-examination, depositions, discovery) — and avoid placing trust ahead of verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay draws a direct lesson for lawyers: devotion to clients can lead to trusting assertions that should be tested. Use discovery and adversarial processes to leave no fact unexamined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of evidence can be decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: Not finding confirming evidence in preserved materials or discovery can itself demonstrate fabrication or falsity; investigators should treat lack of corroboration as important information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Cooke case, the lack of mention of 'Jimmy' in original notes was key. Lawyers and editors should consider negative findings (missing records, absent corroboration) as meaningful and potentially dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not suppress internal misgivings because of a story's appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Colleagues who privately doubt a reporter's account should not refrain from voicing concerns or pressing for verification due to the story's attractiveness or perceived prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several reporters and editors had misgivings but 'suppressed their misgivings in light of the story’s great appeal.' Establish a culture where doubts are aired and investigated rather than silenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and nominations should not override verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The prospect of prizes or recognition (e.g., Pulitzer nomination) must not replace thorough fact-checking; high-level accolades should come only after verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooke's fraud unraveled only because of the Pulitzer nomination prompting background checks. Ensure verification occurs prior to public nominations or awards.
